title: The loan model and the two districts
instructions:
## You review a credit model before launch

A lender's model scores loan applications. The evaluation report splits results by district. Read it, decide whether the model is fair enough to launch, and say what should change.

evidence.title: Evaluation by district
evidence.text:
Overall accuracy: 88%.
District A (urban): approval rate 62%, false rejection rate 8%.
District B (rural): approval rate 31%, false rejection rate 24%.
Training data: 85% of past loans came from District A. Feature list includes "distance to nearest branch" and "mobile money transaction count".

choices.text: The model is fair: overall accuracy is high
choices.feedback: Overall accuracy hides that rural applicants are wrongly rejected three times as often.

choices.text: The model treats the districts differently: creditworthy rural applicants are rejected far more often
choices.feedback: Correct. The false rejection rates differ sharply; that is the harm.
The data may be unrepresentative, but the numbers themselves are the finding.

nodes.title: The cause
nodes.text: What most likely produced the gap?

choices.text: Training data dominated by one district, and features that proxy for location rather than repayment
choices.feedback: Correct. Representation and proxy features are the usual sources of this pattern.
The false rejection rate says the model is wrong about creditworthy rural applicants.
A threefold difference on large groups is not chance.

nodes.title: Which fairness measure?
nodes.text: The lender's goal is that creditworthy applicants get the same chance regardless of district. Which measure matches that goal?

choices.text: Equal opportunity: equal true positive (or false rejection) rates across groups
choices.feedback: Correct. The goal is about creditworthy people being treated alike.

choices.text: Equal approval rates regardless of repayment
choices.feedback: Demographic parity ignores whether applicants can repay; it may not be the right goal for lending.

choices.text: Collect more representative rural data, remove or audit proxy features, retrain, and re-evaluate by group before launch
choices.feedback: Correct. Fix the data and features, then measure again.
That changes volumes, not the gap.
Launching a model known to harm a group is not responsible.

nodes.title: Governance
nodes.text: What should the launch decision require from now on? Before you choose, write the note you would send to the product owner.

prompts.label: Note to the product owner
prompts.hint: Two or three sentences: what the harm is and what must change before launch.

choices.text: A documented evaluation by group, an explanation for rejected applicants, an appeal route, and monitoring after launch
choices.feedback: Correct. Accountability needs documentation, recourse and ongoing measurement.
One person cannot be the whole governance process.

nodes.title: Decision: do not launch yet
nodes.text: You require representative data, a feature audit, group-level evaluation, explanations and an appeal route, with monitoring after launch.

hints: Compare the false rejection rates, not the overall accuracy.
Features correlated with where someone lives can stand in for the district.
Fairness measures encode goals; pick the one that matches the lender's stated goal.

checks.label: Your note explains the harm and the remedy
At least four of the five decisions are right
checks.message: Fewer than four of the five were right. Read the feedback and run the case again.

realityNote: Credit models are one of the most regulated uses of machine learning; group-level evaluation and the right to an explanation are written into several countries' rules and are arriving in African regulation.
